articles.title: Caffeine off the clock: six ways baristas make coffee at home (and one they all hate)
articles.summary: What do people who spend all day making coffee use when off the clock? Their solutions are simpler than you’d expect. The best instant coffees – from from powders to pastes. Sign up for the Filter US newsletter, your weekly guide to buying fewer, better things.
body: Karl Stuebe, barista and co-owner of Home Coffee Roasters in San Francisco, never really clocks out. Every morning at his little home coffee station, he brews a cup and judges it. If it comes out “a little bit bright” (a coffee pro term for “overly acidic”), Stuebe writes a note and tries something different the next day. “I’m always measuring what the quality is like,” he says. “I like to keep testing my palate every day.”

For many baristas and cafe owners like Stuebe, coffee isn’t a drink; it’s a calling. But what do they use to brew at home, away from their $26,000 La Marzocco espresso machines? I asked baristas in the west coast coffee meccas of San Francisco and Portland, Oregon. Here are their favorites, including some surprisingly inexpensive options – and one method they all despise.

Cobi Williams is one of Stuebe’s baristas at Home Coffee Roasters in San Francisco’s Chinatown. Williams chooses his morning brewing method by “how lazy I’m feeling”, he says. On his sleepiest days it’s a French press. “I just wait while it sits.” All you need are coarse grounds and hot water; no paper filters needed, not even electricity. Steep for four minutes, then press.

articles.title: Older women are as varied and individual as we have ever been | Letters
articles.summary: Thank you, Jo Brand, for not offering us a formula for growing older, writes Dr Denise Taylor. Plus a letter from Louise Mothersole. I found Jo Brand’s reflections on approaching 70 wonderfully refreshing ( ‘It’s far too late for me to go to the gym every 10 minutes’: Jo Brand on ageing, raging…
body: We hear so much about ageing well, ageing positively and ageing successfully. We are encouraged to exercise more, eat better, remain productive, find our purpose and keep reinventing ourselves. Much of this advice is well intentioned, but collectively it can make growing older seem like another job we are expected to perform.

As a 69-year-old psychologist who researches and writes about later life, I question this narrative. Of course, looking after our health matters. But ageing isn’t a competition, and we shouldn’t have to demonstrate that we’re making the most of every remaining year.

I was particularly struck by Brand’s comments about older women being treated as though they are all alike. We are as varied, contradictory and individual as we have ever been. Some of us want adventure; others want a quieter life. Some are still working, others are delighted to have left employment behind. And our feelings about ageing can change from one day to the next.

Perhaps what makes Brand’s interview so appealing is that she doesn’t offer us a formula for growing older. She simply describes her experience, with humour, honesty and a willingness to acknowledge what is difficult.
points: Thank you, Jo Brand, for not offering us a formula for growing older, writes Dr Denise Taylor.
We hear so much about ageing well, ageing positively and ageing successfully.

articles.title: Is this the most rubbish Christmas present ever? | Polly Hudson
articles.summary: I thought I knew all about disappointment, having received one of the very worst presents as a child. Then I heard about ‘data gifting’ One Christmas when I was a child, my parents wrapped the presents in shiny paper.
body: The jubilation I felt at pulling off such a stealth move – being basically a master criminal in the manner of those movie jewel thieves who dodge laser tripwires – was almost immediately negated by the sinking realisation I’d ruined my own Christmas. I’d been too impatient to bear the wait, but now, with weeks still to go, all anticipation and excitement had been extinguished. Not least because my main present was – how to put this delicately? – crap.

I always struggled to get up for school, so Santa had stitched me up with an alarm clock. A fun, razzy alarm clock, but an alarm clock all the same. To clarify: no kid wants an alarm clock. It was the very definition of bleak times.

Until this week, I believed this was the most depressing Christmas present in the history of the nativity. But then I heard an advert for a mobile phone provider, which offered the suggestion of “data gifting”. This is where, brimming with festive spirit, you transfer your unused or spare data to somebody else’s device or plan, ho ho ho. A virtual, imaginary present so entirely practical the recipient probably won’t even realise when they use it.

articles.title: What are you yearning for? We took to the streets to find out
articles.summary: Longing for someone – or something – can be even more thrilling than getting what you want. That knowledge has inspired endless movies, but what do real people yearn for? We asked the question in Glasgow.
body: I n a world of instant gratification, is it any surprise that many of us have fallen back in love with the idea of “yearning”? Running counter to much of today’s on-demand culture, yearning melds desire and distance, nostalgia and uncertainty; longing for something, or someone, can sometimes appeal in a way that getting exactly what you want cannot.

The resurgence of yearning – especially in the romantic sense – has been one of the biggest entertainment themes of the last couple of years: from The Summer I Turned Pretty and Heated Rivalry to the latest big-screen adaptation of Sense and Sensibility, the allure of unmet desire and slow-burn love has topped hasty happy-ever-afters. TikTok remains awash with recommendations for those who want to #feeltheyearn.

But yearning encompasses more than just romantic infatuation. You might be pining for a particular place or longing for a different time in life. With this in mind, we took to the streets to ask: what are you yearning for right now?

That knowledge has inspired endless movies, but what do real people yearn for?

articles.title: From the Archives: When Iowa Governor-Elect Rob Sand Was Shot by Steven Meisel for Vogue Italia
articles.summary: Before winning Iowa’s gubernatorial race, Rob Sand was posing with supermodels, wearing Helmut Lang, and walking the Prada runway. Revisit his February 2004 Vogue Italia spread.
body: “Be My Baby,” by Steven Meisel, was originally published in the February 2004 issue of Vogue Italia.

With a fluffed-up quiff and a supermodel on his arm, here’s a look at Iowa’s next governor. Long before Democrat Rob Sand made political history, he was having a very different kind of moment in the spotlight, posing for Steven Meisel in the pages of Vogue Italia.

The year was 2004, and Sand was among the fresh faces who appeared in “Be My Baby,” an editorial in the February issue, photographed by Meisel and styled by Brana Wolf. Alongside Sand was a cast of rising fashion stars, including a young Caroline Trentini, with whom he posed in a series of moody, black-and-white portraits.

The concept centered on a romanticized vision of 1950s youth culture, abounding with the aforementioned rockabilly hair and lots of leather The original Italian introduction described the mood as a collision of bon ton —good manners and traditional propriety—and transgression.
points: Before winning Iowa’s gubernatorial race, Rob Sand was posing with supermodels, wearing Helmut Lang, and walking the Prada runway.

articles.title: No Time to Dye: Jacob Elordi Goes Blonde
articles.summary: Trading his natural brunette for a bleach blonde job, it looks like we’re set to see a big transformation for Jacob Elordi in A24’s “Scapegoat.”
body: The name’s Blonde. James Blonde. Kidding: it’s Jacob Elordi, who has just added another hairstyle to his ever-expanding beauty repertoire. The actor, whose dark, tousled hair has become almost as recognizable as his collection of Bottega Veneta bags, appears to have taken a trip to the bleach bottle.

In photos obtained by Deuxmoi, Elordi was spotted attending a performance of Paranormal Activity on Broadway in New York City on Saturday evening, alongside girlfriend Kendall Jenner. While the Australian actor (who is reportedly in the running to be the next James Bond) kept a low profile in a black beanie, there was no disguising the sandy blonde strands peeking out from beneath it. It’s a significant change-up from his usual chocolate-brown waves, though the hat leaves the full extent of his transformation something of a mystery.

body: The friend link-up at the game may seem like the first in a long time, but back in July, Kloss was one of the special guests at Swift and Kelce’s wedding at Madison Square Garden. “Listen, I try to protect the privacy of my friends’ personal lives,” Kloss later said of the grand event. “But what I will say is that they’re an amazing couple and I’m so happy for them.”

articles.title: Urban Lights & Gucci Nights: An Exclusive Look Inside the LACMA Art + Film Gala
articles.summary: A star-studded night at the museum, where the art world met Hollywood and someone yelled out, “Am I not famous enough?!”
body: The night was young. Very young, as I cruised across Los Angeles to this year’s LACMA Art + Film Gala. I decided to arrive before the usual red-carpet mayhem starts, and because I had gotten ready several hours too early, I was starting to entertain the idea of having a quick nap in my glam and gown. I was wearing a 1930s purple satin bias-cut dress that I won at an auction for considerably less than it was worth. Such a purchase can do wonders for one’s self-esteem: I felt like a million bucks.

This year marked the 15th anniversary of the gala, which honors artists and filmmakers while raising funds to support the museum’s programming. The evening, sponsored by Gucci and co-chaired by Eva Chow and Leonardo DiCaprio, would celebrate Latvian artist Vija Celmins and filmmaker Denis Villeneuve. The art world and Hollywood are not always natural bedfellows, although they have certainly become more comfortable with one another over the years. I was interested to see how the two would behave over dinner.

articles.title: The Wonder—and Weirdness—of Exploring a National Park in the Dark
articles.summary: Once the sun goes down and crowds disperse, nature comes alive. On a trip to Southern Utah, writer Jamie Spain finds a new way to see America’s parks after dark.
body: I’ve spent the majority of my life doing outdoor activities: camping, hiking, biking, kayaking, you name it. It’s intrinsically part of who I am, something that defines my siblings and I so deeply it feels like it’s braided into our DNA.

Perhaps that’s because, when I was just two-and-a-half years old, my parents took my siblings and me on a two-month-long road trip from New York to Arizona, hitting dozens of state and national parks on the way. We still talk about that adventure, lovingly referred to as the Out West Trip. It was the first time I visited Utah’s national parks, known as the Mighty 5: Zion, Arches, Canyonlands, Capitol Reef, and Bryce Canyon.
Once night falls in Utah's national parks, most travelers head back to their campfires or motor lodges—except for those willing to brave the dark and explore their nocturnal side.
